transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-02-19 15:00 PST
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Tom Alvarez (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Luis Gomez (Redwood SE); Sarah Chen (Acme Head of ML), Mark Rivera (Infra), Jenna Li (Product), Omar Patel (Data Eng)
---
[00:00] Tom: hey everyone, thanks for jumping on, quick check, can you hear me ok?
[00:05] Sarah: yes, loud and clear. thanks Tom.
[00:12] Tom: great. quick agenda, we want to go over last week's benchmark numbers, talk about token/sec per dollar, caching savings we saw in the staging pilot and the batching experiments. then we'll map next steps.
[00:25] Priya: hi all, I'll drive the perf bits, Tom will cover the cost model.
[00:30] Jenna: sounds good. we mainly want to see whether the savings are repeatable at scale and if there are risks to shipping caching in prod.
[00:38] Tom: perfect. Priya, you wanna kick off with the benchmark summary?
[00:40] Priya: yeah. so quick summary: last week we ran three 2-hour runs on the dedicated test pool with the opt-6-like model variant you requested (we used the 6B open model quantized to int8 for the runs). run A was baseline no caching, batch size 1, run B was prefix caching enabled with batch size 1, run C was prefix caching + batching to 8.
[01:05] Priya: numbers: baseline tokens/sec was ~120 tokens/sec per instance, cost normalized to our hosted per-token baseline came to about $0.045 per 1k tokens effective; with prefix caching on run B tokens/sec increased to 310 tokens/sec effective (cache hit-rate ~38%), cost dropped to ~$0.018 per 1k tokens. run C (batch 8) moved tokens/sec to ~720 tokens/sec effective but p95/p99 latency increased -- p99 went from ~420ms baseline to ~1.2s with batch 8.
[01:40] Mark: can I pause, those cost numbers are per instance or per-shared-pool? means how are you normalizing to dollars?
[01:47] Tom: good question. we normalized to a per-hour instance cost using the Dedicated pool price we've been using in the pilot sheet (that's in the spreadsheet I sent Friday). essentially tokens/sec * hours and instance hourly rate gives cost per token. we'll share the raw CSVs after the call.
[02:04] Sarah: that 38% hit-rate, that's prefix only right? not KV cache?
[02:10] Priya: correct. that's prefix caching for repeated system+prompt prefixes across requests. we also tried a small KV cache test for session-level history that gave an additional ~10% effective improvement but it was noisier. the big wins were prefix cache for your 3 high-frequency prompt families.
[02:28] Omar: what's noisy in the KV case? is it eviction churn or poor locality?
[02:33] Priya: both. in our short runs we saw eviction churn when sessions are long and diversely distributed; kernel scheduling sometimes flushed entries. with larger capacity of KV store and tuned TTLs the hit-rate improves. Mark, this is likely infra config dependent.
[02:46] Mark: ok noted.
[02:48] Jenna: curious about quality; did quantization to int8 show any regression on your eval prompts?
[02:54] Priya: we ran the standard quality set you gave us, delta in perplexity was small and for the top-critical prompts the human eval samples were within acceptable thresholds. there are edge cases where hallucination slightly increased on a couple of rare prompts; we flagged those in the eval sheet.
[03:12] Tom: to translate to tokens/sec per dollar, think of two knobs: caching which increases tokens served per compute unit without much latency change, and batching which amortizes per-request overhead but increases p99 latency. ideal is to combine caching with small batches (2-4) to get cost down while keeping p99 under your SLO.
[03:32] Sarah: what's the sweet spot you saw?
[03:34] Priya: for your workload the sweet spot in preliminary tests was prefix caching + batch 4. tokens/sec jumped to ~410 tokens/sec and p99 stayed ~620-700ms which you said is acceptable for async UX flows.
[03:48] Sarah: for chat flows early in the funnel we need sub-300ms p99 for interactive, but for downstream generation 600-800ms is fine.
[03:57] Tom: makes sense. we can map routes: interactive endpoints use batch 1 + small cache TTLs, long-running generation use batch 4 and aggressive caching. that's exactly where routing policies in the platform help.
[04:10] Mark: what's the impact on cost if we split interactive vs batch routes? any estimate?
[04:15] Tom: quick back-of-envelope: if interactive 20% of traffic stays at baseline tokens/sec 120 but hosted on reserved instances it's about $X per 1M tokens; the other 80% with caching+batch4 gets effective tokens/sec 410 which reduces cost by ~55% compared to baseline. overall blended saving ~40-45% on token cost. we'll show the blended numbers in the spreadsheet.
[04:38] Jenna: can we get numbers per model variant? like 6B quantized vs 13B fp16?
[04:44] Priya: yes, we have a 13B run too but the numbers are obviously different: 13B fp16 baseline tokens/sec was ~55, with caching+batch4 it went to ~210 tokens/sec but cost per hour is higher; the unit economics still favor 6B quantized for many prompt families unless quality mandates 13B.
[05:04] Sarah: okay. one risk is consistency — if caching keying changes results between requests, we could see user-facing regressions. how stable is the prefix caching keying?
[05:14] Priya: we key on normalized prefix including normalized system prompt and canonicalized user prefix; we also support a test mode where cache is warm but not served to production responses so you can audit mismatches. we recommend running audit mode for a week before flip.
[05:29] Omar: about audit mode, how do we compare outputs? diff metric or human sampling?
[05:34] Priya: both; automated diffing based on embed-similarity and token-level deltas for deterministic areas, plus a small human sample for semantic checks. we'll provide the audit tool config.
[05:44] Tom: quick note on economics: caching savings are multiplicative with batching but you get diminishing returns with large batch sizes because cache hits become batched together — the marginal benefit of moving from batch 4 to batch 8 is smaller but latency cost grows.
[06:00] Mark: what about startup cold-cache scenario? do we lose the savings initially?
[06:04] Priya: yes cold-start effects matter. in our 24-hour run we saw hit-rate ramp over first 6-12 hours on your traffic shape. that's why we recommend seeding cache via a warmup job or pre-warming frequently-used prefixes during deploy.
[06:18] Sarah: warmup job — how invasive is that?
[06:21] Priya: it's just a batch process hitting the service with the canonical prefixes at controlled rate. low risk. we can share a script.
[06:28] Jenna: ok. on the cost model in the sheet, there were some line-items like 'opportunity cost' and 'reserved instance amortization', we need to understand assumptions.
[06:36] Tom: yep we'll annotate each assumption. main levers are instance hourly price, average tokens/session, and cache hit-rate. we surfaced sensitivity analysis for hit-rate +/- 10% in the sheet.
[06:47] Omar: can we talk briefly about SLAs: if we push caching heavily, do you still guarantee p99 targets?
[06:51] Priya: platform SLOs are configurable; caching itself doesn't break p99 targets but batching does. we can set route-level p99 goals and Redwood's smart router will avoid batching on routes that need strict latency. also for Dedicated we can reserve more capacity to keep p99 low under load.
[07:08] Mark: any network or infra constraints? we run in GCP and want to keep traffic inside our VPC for Private mode.
[07:14] Tom: for the pilot you're in Dedicated hosted mode with VPC peering. Private deployment is available but more involved. for now caching and batching run in the Redwood runtime inside the dedicated pool with peered network. if you move to Private we can still do the same caching strategies.
[07:27] Sarah: do you have SOC2 / audit implications for caching session data?
[07:31] Priya: yes we support config to not cache PII by default; caching keys can be filtered and we integrate with KMS for encryption at rest. our security docs cover audit logs and retention. we'll attach the security pack.
[07:42] Tom: ok, turning to questions from your side — Jenna?
[07:45] Jenna: yes, two quick ones: 1) how do refunds or billing adjustments work if pilot costs mismatch? 2) what's the expected uplift in throughput if we switch to Dedicated with autoscaling?
[07:55] Tom: for pilot billing we typically have a consumption report and we can prorate adjustments if metrics diverge from assumptions; we'll work with finance on that. autoscaling uplift depends on instance counts and model peformance — rough rule: doubling instance count gives near-linear throughput until you hit other bottlenecks like I/O. we'll model that in the spreadsheet.
[08:16] Sarah: can we get a recommended config to try in staging this week? a single YAML or a checklist would be great.
[08:22] Priya: yes, we'll send a recommended config: prefix cache enabled (TTL 24h), KV cache for sessions (TTL 6h), batch size 4 for non-interactive routes, audit mode enabled for two interactive routes.
[08:33] Tom: action items recap: I'll send updated cost spreadsheet + raw CSVs; Priya will send recommended config and script to seed cache; Mark will run the 24-hour benchmark; Sarah to pick the 3 prompt families.
[08:44] Mark: one more infra note — we noticed some kernel preemption spikes at high batch sizes during run C, we should capture those logs.
[08:51] Priya: yes we'll include scheduler traces. Luis will correlate with the perf CSV.
[08:55] Luis: yup I'll stitch those and include a short doc.
[09:00] Sarah: thanks all. next sync same time next week?
[09:05] Tom: let's tentatively schedule, and we'll send a calendar invite. thanks everyone.
[09:10] (call ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional word substitutions (e.g., "KV cash" in early drafts), timestamps approximate every few minutes, some speaker overlaps.
